issues.claim: The runtime performs static type initialization once and in a thread-safe way, so this Singleton needs no hand-written locking.
issues.problem: The claim is correct CLR behaviour, but neither cited page supports it. The auto-implemented-properties excerpt only shows that auto-properties can have initializers. The expression-bodied page covers only expression-body syntax. The generator notes already flag this gap. A reader cannot verify the thread-safety claim from the listed sources.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the static constructors page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/static-constructors) to links, with linkTitles in both locales, and re-check that it states the once-only static initialization guarantee. Alternatively, drop the thread-safety sentence.

issues.problem: The URL redirects to the lambda-operator page. Its 'Expression body definition' section does support the claim, but the page title is 'Lambda operator' and does not match the link title.
issues.suggestedFix: Use https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-operator#expression-body-definition and title it 'Expression body definition' / 'Определение тела выражения'.

issues.claim: How many times does the expression after `=>` in a property declaration run, and how many times does a property initializer run?
issues.problem: The hint points straight at the contrast between `=>` and an initializer, which nearly gives away the answer. The title and prompt already say a new object is created on every access.
issues.suggestedFix: Soften it: 'Compare how many times each member of Counter is evaluated. What decides how often a new object is created?' Use the equivalent wording in Russian.

issues.problem: Verified against the numbered source: line 11 is `    public static Counter Instance => new Counter();`, and it is the bug. The sandbox run of the fixed source gave 3, matching fixedExpect. No issue here; noted for completeness.

The excerpt of 'Handling and raising events' never says that .NET events implement the Observer pattern. It describes subscribing and raising only. The generator notes admit this was unchecked. The claim 'event implements Observer' is therefore not shown to be supported by this page.
issues.suggestedFix: Remove this link, or replace it with a page that says it explicitly. Re-check that the observer-design-pattern page ties events to the Observer pattern. Its excerpt only calls events 'more idiomatic' for simple notification.

issues.claim: yield statement page cited for 'yield return and Iterator'
issues.problem: The excerpt shows how yield works and that iterators return IEnumerable<T>/IEnumerator<T>. It never mentions the Iterator design pattern or the compiler-generated state machine claimed in the explanation.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the C# iterators page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/iterators) if it supports the state-machine claim, or reword the explanation to what the yield page states.

issues.claim: A `Func<T>` delegate and Strategy; Strategy 'can be passed as a delegate (`Func<T>`, `Comparison<T>`...) instead of an interface'
issues.problem: No cited link supports the delegate-as-Strategy claim. Also, `Func<T>` is a parameterless delegate returning T, which is an odd example of a Strategy. Typical strategies take arguments, such as `Func<T,TResult>` or `Comparison<T>`.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword option b as 'A delegate (for example `Func<T, TResult>`) and Strategy' in both locales. Add a source such as the Comparison<T> API page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.comparison-1) or a Strategy-with-delegates article. Update the answer and explanation to match.

issues.claim: Which of these constructs change how objects interact with each other, and which only control how a block of code runs?
issues.problem: The hint effectively names the wrong options (lock and using) by saying they only control how a block runs, so it gives away part of the answer.
